news_drafts.headline: Scottish Borders used its own cash instead of £111.3m of borrowing at March 2026, down from £127.9m
news_drafts.lead:
Scottish Borders Council ended 2025/26 having used its own spare cash, rather than taking out loans, to pay for £111.3m of spending on long-lasting assets such as buildings and roads. A year earlier the figure was £127.9m. The figures are in the council's annual treasury management report (how it borrows, invests spare cash and manages the risks of both), which went to its Audit Committee on 21 September 2026.

The papers measure this against the capital financing requirement, the total the council has spent on long-lived assets that it has not yet paid for, in effect its underlying need to borrow. Using cash in place of a loan is known as internal borrowing, which saves interest but uses up the council's own cushion. The report says the council "has again, where possible, deferred borrowing using surplus cash rather than undertaking new borrowing". It describes this as a deliberate policy and puts the fall in the figure down to lower expected capital demands.

An appendix to the report compares the requirement one year ahead with the council's external debt, the total of all loans it owes. On that basis the council "remains under-borrowed by £65.9m at the end of 2025/26", the paper says.

news_drafts.headline: Scottish Borders pension fund cash deficit widens as pensioners outnumber active members
news_drafts.lead: The Scottish Borders Council pension fund faces a structural cash deficit as pensioner numbers have grown to exceed active member numbers for the first time, with one pensioner now for every active member employed. Over the year to June 2026, pension payments and costs of £366m outstripped contributions by £9m, a shortfall the fund must cover from investment returns and reserves. Pensioner membership has risen 28% over five years while active members grew just 2.9%, a demographic shift that began when the fund matured in 2013/14. This year the fund delivered a 5.7% investment return, the lowest among Scotland's 11 local government pension schemes and well below its 12.3% benchmark; the fund has since terminated underperforming equity managers and committed to changes. Despite the cash flows, Audit Scotland's draft annual report concluded the fund has effective governance and financial management arrangements in place. The council's employer contribution rate was cut to 17% from 18.5% following a strong 134% funding valuation in 2023.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Strategic Housing Investment Plan 2027-2032 Report for Exec Committee
findings.headline: Completed affordable homes will generate additional council tax income of £1.052m-£1.816m to the council over 2027-2032 depending on delivery scenario achieved
findings.detail: The council has modelled the fiscal benefit of development completion. Under the realistic 705-home scenario (650 net council-tax-paying households), the authority will receive £1.052m additional council tax income over the five-year period. Under the ambitious 1,184-home scenario, this rises to £1.816m, improving the council's medium-term fiscal position from one-off capital investment.
findings.matters: Shows the ongoing financial benefit to council from successful housing delivery, demonstrating how capital investment generates improved revenue streams in future years; this is material to council's medium-term financial planning
findings.figures: £1.052m additional council tax (705-home scenario), £1.816m additional council tax (1,184-home scenario), both over April 2027-March 2032
findings.quote: Should all the potential new homes be delivered (1,122 from 1,184 figure), then an estimated £1.816m additional income from Council Tax could be generated for the Council over period 1 April 2027 to 31 March 2032, based on current funding assumption figures (650 from 705 figure), then an estimated £1.052m additional income from Council Tax.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Strategic Housing Investment Plan 2027-2032 Report for Exec Committee
findings.headline: Realistic delivery rate of 141 homes per year over 2027-2032 represents significant increase from Scottish Borders' 20-year historical average of 125 homes per year
findings.detail: The council notes that realistic delivery of 705 homes over five years (141 homes/year) presents an "unprecedented challenge and opportunity" when compared with the authority's long-term performance of 125 homes/year average over the past 20 years. This context shows the plan requires elevated performance from council and partners relative to established delivery track record.
findings.matters: Shows the council is stretching historical performance, which introduces delivery risk; however, the council has also delivered over 2,000 homes across 18 previous SHIP submissions, demonstrating capability to deliver at scale over time
findings.figures: 141 homes/year target vs 125 homes/year 20-year average; 2,000+ homes delivered over 18 previous SHIP submissions since 2007
findings.quote: especially in the context of Scottish Borders affordable housing delivery annual average of 125 over the last 20 years

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Strategic Housing Investment Plan 2027-2032 Report for Exec Committee
findings.headline: Delivery of plan is explicitly acknowledged as dependent on variables largely beyond council control, including RSL site acquisition, government decisions, and external political factors
findings.detail: The council states in its risk section that SHIP delivery "is largely dependent upon a number of variables not least of which relate to resource and other political and organisation decision making processes, most of which are beyond the control of the Council." Successful delivery requires RSL partners to secure and maintain development sites and depends on continuation of government funding and external approvals.
findings.matters: A lender benefits from transparent disclosure of risk factors and the council's candid assessment that meaningful parts of its strategy depend on factors outside its direct control; this honesty about dependency and risk is a governance strength
findings.quote: Delivery of the SHIP is largely dependent upon a number of variables not least of which relate to resource and other political and organisation decision making processes, most of which are beyond the control of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Strategic Housing Investment Plan 2027-2032 Report for Exec Committee
findings.headline: Council commits up to £3.5m annual Second Homes Council Tax revenue to housing delivery with available balances of £1.728m-£3.317m maintained across plan period
findings.detail: The council is deploying discretionary Second Homes Council Tax funding (annual commitments ranging from £250k to £2.474m) to support delivery. The Council's published financial table shows available balances after commitments increasing from £1.728m in 2028/29 to £3.317m in 2029/30, demonstrating the funding stream is financially sustainable over the 2026/27-2029/30 period and the council maintains adequate reserves.
findings.matters: Shows how the council is using limited discretionary revenue to advance strategic priorities, and confirms it is maintaining adequate balance reserves to absorb demand or cost pressures
findings.figures: Up to £3.5m Second Homes Council Tax funding over SHIP period; available balances £2.273m (2026/27), £1.904m (2027/28), £1.728m (2028/29), £3.317m (2029/30)
findings.quote: The SHIP also assumes use of up to £3.5m Second Homes Council Tax funding from the Council and up to £160m of estimated private borrowing by the RSLs over the period of the SHIP to 2032.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Strategic Housing Investment Plan 2027-2032 Report for Exec Committee
findings.headline: Scottish Government confirms £74.230m Affordable Housing Supply Programme funding to Scottish Borders for 2026/27-2029/30 at £17.743m rising to £19.388m annually
findings.detail: Core funding is secured through 2029/30 with confirmed annual allocations: £17.743m (2026/27), £18.275m (2027/28), £18.823m (2028/29), £19.388m (2029/30). This £74.230m forms the foundation of the plan, supplemented by Council discretionary revenue and RSL borrowing. Funding beyond 2029/30 is assumed but not yet confirmed.
findings.matters: This is the committed funding base for the council's own and RSL partner delivery; clarity on funding continuity is essential for a lender assessing council's ability to deliver on housing objectives

daily_post.headline: Company operates at perfect break-even with turnover matched exactly by costs in both years
daily_post.lead: Perfect annual break-even suggests costs are absorbed elsewhere (by council staff and services) and the entity generates no financial surplus, leaving no operational margin for variation or contingency.
